LIABILITY AUDIT · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · OPEN SOURCE

What in your app could cost you a fine, a chargeback or a surprise bill?

Pick your project folder or a built site. Liability Audit reads it locally and reports the common, cheap-to-fix exposures. It checks for trackers with no consent step, subscriptions with no renewal or cancellation terms, a missing privacy notice or terms, affiliate links and AI with no disclosure, and tax, legal or medical tools with no "not advice" line. It also checks for live keys in the tree, LLM endpoints anyone can spend on your key, cloud with no budget alarm and strong-copyleft dependencies. Each finding shows where it is, the law or rule behind it, and the fix.

Nothing is uploaded: files are read by this page in your browser and never leave your device. Findings are observations to check, not legal advice.

1. Choose what to scan

2. What it found

3. Keep it checked: CLI and CI

node cli.mjs scan .                       # text report
node cli.mjs scan . --format md           # a PR comment
node cli.mjs scan . --format sarif > la.sarif   # GitHub code scanning
node cli.mjs scan . --fail-on high        # CI gate
node cli.mjs rules                        # every rule and the law behind it

Read what a small app can be liable for, and how to check for the reasoning behind each rule and the limits of an automated scan.

Questions

Does a clean report mean my app is compliant?

No. It means none of the patterns this tool looks for were found in the files you gave it. It cannot see your servers, your contracts, what your vendors do with data, or what your pages say in images. It is a checklist that finds the common, cheap-to-fix problems early; it is not legal advice and not a compliance certificate.

Why does an LLM endpoint without a rate limit count as a liability?

If your server calls a model on your own API key and anyone can reach that endpoint, one abusive user, a scraper or a stuck agent loop can run up the bill, and the provider charges the account owner. A per-user budget or rate limit in front of the call caps that exposure.

Is my code uploaded?

No. The page reads the folder or text you choose in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI reads local files and makes no network request.

Can I run it in CI?

Yes. node cli.mjs scan . --fail-on high exits 1 on any high-severity finding, --format md writes a PR comment, and --format sarif produces a file GitHub code scanning can show inline.

It pattern-matches files: it can miss problems and flag non-problems, and a clear report is not a finding that anything is lawful. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for your own compliance. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use. Product and law names are used descriptively; this project is not affiliated with any vendor named in its rules.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The files you choose are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (scan_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Related: LLM Spend Guard enforces the spend cap this audit looks for, Affiliate Disclosure Checker checks one post's disclosure placement in depth, EU AI Act Risk Checker works out your AI Act tier, and Lockfile License Check lists every dependency licence.

What a small app can be liable for, and how to check

Most small apps never meet a regulator. The ones that get hurt are usually hurt by something cheap to have fixed: a chargeback wave from a subscription nobody knew renewed, a privacy complaint about an analytics pixel, a leaked key that ran up a five-figure cloud bill. Each of these leaves a trace in the code, so a scan can catch it before launch.

The rules, and why each exists

RuleExposureWhere it comes from
tracker-without-consentFines and complaints for tracking before consentEU ePrivacy rules and GDPR; UK PECR; opt-out rights in several US state privacy laws
personal-data-no-privacy-noticeCollecting data with no noticeGDPR Articles 13–14; California's CalOPPA; app-store rules
subscription-no-renewal-termsRefunds, chargebacks, regulator action over recurring chargesUS ROSCA and state automatic-renewal laws (for example California Business and Professions Code §17600 and following); EU and UK pre-contract information rules
payments-no-termsNo refund policy, liability cap or acceptable-use rule to rely onContract law; payment processors' expectations
affiliate-links-no-disclosureDeceptive endorsementFTC Endorsement Guides, 16 CFR Part 255; UK CAP Code; affiliate programme terms
ai-output-no-disclosureUndisclosed AI interaction and unlabelled generated contentEU AI Act Article 50 (from 2 August 2026); California's B.O.T. Act
advice-without-disclaimerReliance claims on a tax, legal, medical or financial toolNegligent misrepresentation; a stated limit of reliance is the usual mitigation
comparison-no-trademark-noticeImplied affiliation with a named productTrademark law: nominative fair use is safest with a non-affiliation line
copyleft-dependencyLicence breach in a closed or conflicting productGPL, AGPL and SSPL terms
secret-in-treeA stolen key spends on your accountProvider terms generally make the account owner liable for usage
llm-endpoint-no-spend-controlAnyone who reaches the endpoint can spend your model budgetThe provider bills the key's owner
llm-call-no-output-capEach call's worst case is the model's full outputPer-token billing
cloud-no-budget-alarmNo ceiling on a cloud bill, and no warningClouds bill usage with no default cap
no-licenseNobody has rights to use the code; contributors' rights unclearCopyright default

Every finding is phrased as an observation with its evidence, a file and line, so you can check it. None is a determination that something is or is not lawful.

What we found running it on our own projects

On 16 October 2026 we ran node cli.mjs sweep over this repository's 1,274 product directories and 506 research projects. It took about 14 seconds.

  • The product portfolio: 4 low-severity findings, all comparison pages naming another product without a non-affiliation line. These are static, browser-only tools that collect nothing and carry their disclaimers, which is the house rule. On a portfolio built to that rule, the scan's job is to keep it true as it grows.
  • The one-click deploy templates: the OpenTofu templates that deploy an app into a stranger's AWS, Google Cloud or Azure account declared no budget or cost alarm. That is the financial exposure the rule exists for, and it lands on the person deploying. The same change that added this tool fixed it: each template now takes an optional alert address (or, on Google Cloud, a billing account) and creates a monthly budget that warns at 80% of actual and 100% of forecast spend.
  • Getting the rules right took the sweep. The first version raised 153 findings, almost all false. Titles like "Pallet vs Carton" read as competitor comparisons. "Do I need to register for GST?" read as a sign-up form. Pattern lists inside scanners read as live LLM calls. A password box for an API key read as a login. Each is now a test case.

What a scan cannot see

  • Whether your privacy notice is true, or what your vendors do with data.
  • Your contracts, employment, tax registration, or sector licensing (health, finance, insurance).
  • Text in images, a CMS or a database; anything behind a login.
  • Runtime behaviour: the scan reads files, it does not watch traffic. For spend, pair it with a guard in the request path such as LLM Spend Guard.

Run it continuously

Add node cli.mjs scan . --fail-on high to CI so a new high-severity exposure fails the pull request. Post --format md as a PR comment, or upload --format sarif to GitHub code scanning to see findings inline. For a monorepo, sweep gives one row per app. The repository's AGENT.md is a playbook for an AI coding agent: run the scan, triage each finding against the code, fix what is clearly a fix, and bring the judgment calls to a person.

Questions

Which liabilities can an automated scan find?

The ones that leave a trace in files: a tracker script without a consent manager, subscription checkout code without renewal and cancellation wording, data-collecting forms without a privacy notice, affiliate links before any disclosure, AI calls without a statement that AI is used, live keys, LLM endpoints with no limit, cloud IaC with no budget, and copyleft licences in a lockfile.

Which can it not find?

Anything that depends on facts outside the files: what your vendors do with data, whether your privacy notice is accurate, contracts, employment, tax registration, sector rules such as health or finance licensing, and anything in images or a CMS. A clean scan is not a compliance opinion.

Why treat runaway cloud or AI spend as a liability?

Because it is one: the account owner owes the bill. A leaked key, an endpoint anyone can drive on your model key, or an autoscaler with no budget alarm can produce a charge larger than the business earns in a year, and providers do not have to forgive it.
